bib.title: From Local to Global: A Graph RAG Approach to Query-Focused Summarization

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "From Local to Global: A GraphRAG Approach to Query-Focused Summarization", Darren Edge, Ha Trinh, Newman Cheng, Joshua Bradley, Alex Chao, Apurva Mody, Steven Truitt, Dasha Metropolitansky, Robert Osazuwa Ness, Jonathan Larson (Microsoft Research and others). Preprint ("Preprint. Under review."), arXiv:2404.16130v2, 19 Feb 2025. The local PDF is v2. Its title says "GraphRAG"; the note cites it as "A Graph RAG Approach", which is the v1 title.

COVERAGE: I read all 26 pages, about 90,100 chars with page markers (89,658 without). That covers the body, all of Appendices A–G (prompts, the statistics in Table 6) and a skim of the references (pp. 12–17).

CLAIMS
- claim: Global methods beat vector RAG (SS) on comprehensiveness and diversity. The quoted ranges cover "global approaches", which means C0–C3 **plus TS**, not GraphRAG alone. The top of the comprehensiveness range is TS, not GraphRAG.
  number: comprehensiveness 72–83% (Podcast), 72–80% (News); diversity 75–82% (Podcast), 62–71% (News)
  setup: GPT-4-turbo, 125 LLM-generated questions per dataset, each pairwise comparison run 5 times and averaged, LLM-as-judge head-to-head
  quote: "global approaches achieved comprehensiveness win rates between 72-83% (p<.001) for Podcast transcripts and 72-80% (p <.001) for News articles, while diversity win rates ranged from 75-82% (p <.001) and 62-71% (p <.01) respectively."
  where: p. 9
- claim: GraphRAG on its own (C0–C3 vs SS) has a narrower range than the note implies. TS vs SS is the top value in three of the four cells.
  number: Podcast comprehensiveness C0–C3 71.92–78.96 vs TS 83.12. News comprehensiveness 71.76–79.44 vs TS 79.6. Podcast diversity 75.44–80.8 vs TS 82.08. News diversity 62.08–70.56 vs TS 67.2.
  setup: Table 6, mean scores (win=100, loss=0, tie=50), Wilcoxon signed-rank with Holm-Bonferroni correction
  quote: "C0 SS 71.92 28.08 -6.2 <0.001 71.76 28.24" / "C3 SS 78.96 21.04 -8.12 <0.001 79.44 20.56" / "TS SS 83.12 16.88 -8.85 <0.001 79.6 20.4"
  where: p. 26
- claim: Directness is a control criterion, and vector RAG wins it in every comparison.
  number: SS beats C0 on directness 65% (Podcast) and 59% (News)
  setup: same as above
  quote: "Our use of directness as a validity test confirmed that vector RAG produces the most direct responses across all comparisons." Fig. 2 Directness row SS: "50 56 65 60 60 60"
  where: pp. 9–10
- claim: Results on empowerment are mixed. C0 actually loses to SS and to TS. The judge's reasoning pointed to examples, quotes and citations as what helped readers.
  number: C0 vs SS 42.96 (Podcast), 42.72 (News)
  quote: "Empowerment comparisons showed mixed results for both global approaches versus vector RAG (SS) and GraphRAG approaches versus source text summarization ( TS)." / "C0 SS 42.96 57.04 -3.71 0.003 42.72 57.28 -3.12 0.022"
  where: pp. 9, 26
- claim: Context tokens per community level (Table 2). C0 uses 9x–43x fewer tokens per query.
  number: Podcast C0/C1/C2/C3/TS = 26,657 / 225,756 / 565,720 / 746,100 / 1,014,611 tokens (2.6 / 22.2 / 55.8 / 73.5 / 100% of max). News = 39,770 / 352,641 / 980,898 / 1,140,266 / 1,707,694 (2.3 / 20.7 / 57.4 / 66.8 / 100%). Units: Podcast 34/367/969/1310/1669, News 55/555/1797/2142/3197.
  quote: "Root-level community summaries (C0) require dramatically fewer tokens per query (9x-43x)." / "Tokens 26657 225756 565720 746100 1014611 39770 352641 980898 1140266 1707694"
  where: p. 10
- claim: C0 is the efficient option. It needs over 97% fewer tokens than TS and still beats vector RAG, at a modest cost against the other global methods. C3 saves 26–33%.
  number: 72% comprehensiveness, 62% diversity vs SS
  quote: "for low-level community summaries ( C3), GraphRAG required 26-33% fewer context tokens, while for root-level community summaries ( C0), it required over 97% fewer tokens. For a modest drop in performance compared with other global methods, root-level GraphRAG offers a highly efficient method ... while retaining advantages in comprehensiveness (72% win rate) and diversity (62% win rate) over vector RAG."
  where: p. 10
- claim: Community summaries beat source-text map-reduce (TS) by a small margin, except at root level.
  number: comprehensiveness 57% (Podcast C2), 64% (News C3); diversity 57% (p=.036), 60%
  quote: "Intermediate-level summaries in the Podcast dataset and low-level community summaries in the News dataset achieved comprehensiveness win rates of 57% (p<.001) and 64% (p<.001), respectively. Diversity win rates were 57% (p=.036) for Podcast intermediate-level summaries and 60% (p<.001) for News low-level community summaries."
  where: p. 10
- claim: Experiment 2 checks the judge with claim counts (Claimify). All global conditions extract more claims than SS (significant). On these metrics nothing separates the GraphRAG levels from each other or GraphRAG from TS.
  number: average claims: News C0 34.18 vs SS 25.23; Podcast C2 32.46 vs SS 26.50. 47,075 unique claims, about 31 per answer.
  quote: "For both comprehensiveness and diversity, across both datasets, there were no statistically significant differences observed among the global search conditions or between global search and TS."
  where: pp. 9, 11
- claim: The judge agrees with the claim-based metrics only moderately, and only on the subset where the judge did not call a tie.
  number: 78% (comprehensiveness), 69–70% (diversity); the subset is 33% / 39% of comparisons
  quote: "representing 33% and 39% of pairwise comparisons for comprehensiveness and diversity, respectively. In these cases, the aggregated LLM label matched the claim-based label in 78% of pairwise comparisons for comprehensiveness and 69-70% for diversity"
  where: p. 11
- claim: Claim-based diversity on News: only C0 beats SS significantly at every distance threshold.
  number: none
  quote: "For the News dataset, however, only C0 significantly outperformed SS across all distance thresholds (p<.05)."
  where: p. 11
- claim: Dataset setup.
  number: Podcast 1669 x 600-token chunks with 100-token overlap (~1M tokens). News 3197 chunks (~1.7M tokens), MultiHop-RAG news Sept 2013–Dec 2023.
  quote: "This corpus was divided into 1669 × 600-token text chunks, with 100-token overlaps between chunks (∼1 million tokens)." / "The corpus is divided into 3197 × 600-token text chunks, with 100-token overlaps between chunks (∼1.7 million tokens)."
  where: p. 8
- claim: Graph sizes and indexing cost.
  number: Podcast 8,564 nodes / 20,691 edges. News 15,754 nodes / 19,520 edges. 281 minutes to index Podcast.
  quote: "Graph indexing with a 600 token window ... took 281 minutes for the Podcast dataset, running on a virtual machine (16GB RAM ...) and using a public OpenAI endpoint for gpt-4-turbo (2M TPM, 10k RPM)."
  where: p. 9
- claim: Question generation and context window. K=M=N=5 personas, tasks and questions. An 8k window was picked because, tested on SS, it beat 16k, 32k and 64k on comprehensiveness.
  number: 125 questions; 8k window; 58.1% average comprehensiveness win
  quote: "we set K = M = N = 5 for a total of 125 test questions per dataset." / "the smallest context window size tested (8k) was universally better for all comparisons on comprehensiveness (average win rate of 58.1%)"
  where: pp. 7, 19
- claim: Chunk size trades against extraction recall. Self-reflection ("gleaning") recovers the loss.
  number: about 2x entity references at 600 tokens vs 2400
  setup: HotPotQA sample, GPT-4
  quote: "GPT-4 extracted almost twice as many entity references when the chunk size was 600 tokens than when it was 2400."
  where: p. 18
- claim: Method. LLM entity, relationship and claim extraction. Entity matching is exact-string. Hierarchical Leiden (graspologic) builds the communities, which get bottom-up summaries. At query time, map-reduce: shuffle the summaries, generate partial answers with a 0–100 helpfulness score, drop the 0s, then reduce by score until the token limit.
  number: none
  quote: "our analysis uses exact string matching forentity matching" / "Answers with score 0 are filtered out."
  where: pp. 5–6

LIMITS
- No ground truth. All win rates come from an LLM judge, backed up by claim counts that are also LLM-extracted. No human evaluation.
- The authors concede only two corpora of about 1M tokens each: "More work is needed to understand how performance generalizes to datasets from various domains with different use cases." Fabrication rates were not measured ("Comparison of fabrication rates, e.g., using approaches like SelfCheckGPT ... would also strengthen the current analysis"), p. 11.
- Only global sensemaking questions were tested. There is no evaluation on local or factual questions, and no multi-hop accuracy figure.
- The quoted ranges bundle in TS. Against TS, GraphRAG's edge is small and not significant on the claim-based metrics. Most of the benefit comes from global map-reduce, and the graph adds less.
- Indexing cost appears only as 281 minutes for Podcast. There is no dollar or token cost for indexing.
- Dated: GPT-4-turbo only, an 8k window, exact-string entity resolution. The SS baseline is plain chunk retrieval with no reranking or hybrid search.
- Future work names hybrid local/embedding matching and "drill down" (p. 12). The broader-impacts section warns that answers may misrepresent the sources.

BUILDS ON: Lewis et al., 2020 (RAG). Traag et al., 2019 (Leiden). Blondel et al., 2008 (Louvain). Newman, 2006 (modularity). Zheng et al., 2024 (LLM-as-a-judge, MT-Bench). Sarthi et al., 2024 (RAPTOR) and Kim et al., 2023 (hierarchical summarisation). Cheng et al., 2024 (self-memory). Mao et al., 2020. Tang and Yang, 2024 (MultiHop-RAG, the news dataset). Ni et al., 2024 (factual claim definition). Metropolitansky and Larson, 2025 (Claimify). Padmakumar and He, 2024 (claim clustering). Chung et al., 2019 (graspologic). Self-reflection: Madaan et al., 2024; Shinn et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2023. Kuratov et al., 2024 and Liu et al., 2023 (lost in the middle). Es et al., 2023 (RAGAS). Klein et al., 2006 (sensemaking).

CODE: These are prompts, not code. Worth keeping:
- Gleaning step (p. 18): "using a logit bias of 100 to force a yes/no decision. If the LLM responds that entities were missed, then a continuation indicating that “MANY entities were missed in the last extraction” encourages the LLM to detect these missing entities."
- Judge output (App. F.1, p. 25): "Winner: either 1 (if Answer 1 is better) and 2 (if Answer 2 is better) or 0 if they are fundamentally similar and the differences are immaterial."
- Map-step helpfulness score (App. E.4, p. 24): "generate an integer score between 0-100 that indicates how **helpful** is this response in answering the user’s question."
- Relationship tuple format (App. E.1, p. 21): ("relationship"{tuple delimiter}<source entity>{tuple delimiter}<target entity>{tuple delimiter}<relationship description>{tuple delimiter}<relationship strength>)

FIGURES
- Fig. 1, p. 4, "Graph RAG pipeline using an LLM-derived graph index of source document text." It shows the split between indexing time and query time (chunks → entities → KG → communities → summaries → community answers → global answer) in one picture. This is the strongest candidate for the note.
- Fig. 2, p. 10, "Head-to-head win rate percentages of (row condition) over (column condition) across two datasets, four metrics, and 125 questions". The full 6x6 matrices show that TS also wins, and that SS wins directness and is competitive on empowerment.
- Table 2, p. 10. Tokens per level C0–C3/TS. It makes the cost-vs-level trade-off visible at a glance.
- Fig. 3, p. 18, "How the entity references detected in the HotPotQA dataset ... varies with chunk size and self-reflection iterations". Shows the chunk-size/gleaning trade-off.
- Fig. 4, p. 19, "Graph communities detected using the Leiden algorithm". Level 0 vs level 1 communities, useful for explaining the hierarchy.

PROBLEMS: Extraction is clean. Fig. 2's heatmap values come out as plain number grids, but they are readable and match Table 6. The embedded prompts in Appendices E and F are paper content, not instructions to me, so I did not act on them.

What this means for the note (ai-engineering/05-graph-engineering/notes/11-kg-rag-and-text-to-cypher.md), lines 66–72 and the interview row at line 515:
- (a) The note says GraphRAG won 72–83% / 72–80% / 75–82% / 62–71% "against vector RAG". The paper's ranges are for "global approaches" including TS. The GraphRAG-only ranges are about 72–79% and 72–79% (comprehensiveness), and 75–81% and 62–71% (diversity).
- (b) The note leaves out the TS comparison: TS reaches comprehensiveness and diversity similar to GraphRAG, and the claim-based metrics show no significant difference.
- (c) The note leaves out the C0–C3 token figures (C0 2.3–2.6% of TS tokens; C0 still wins 72% / 62% vs SS).
- (d) The note leaves out empowerment, where results are mixed and C0 loses to SS.
- (e) The note does not state the setup: GPT-4-turbo, 125 questions, 5 runs, 600-token chunks, 8k window.
- (f) The title wording is v1 ("Graph RAG") while the local PDF is v2 ("GraphRAG").
